value.overview: The Tahiti Petrel (Pseudobulweria rostrata) is a medium-sized tropical seabird of the family Procellariidae. It spends most of its life at sea and comes ashore mainly at night to breed on remote Pacific islands. Despite its name, it is not restricted to Tahiti. The species breeds across parts of French Polynesia, Melanesia, American Samoa, Fiji, and New Caledonia, and disperses widely across the tropical Pacific outside the breeding season.
value.classification: The Tahiti Petrel belongs to the petrel and shearwater family Procellariidae in the order Procellariiformes. It is the only widely recognized species in the genus Pseudobulweria, although regional subspecies have been described.
value.identification: This petrel has dark brown upperparts, a paler face and throat, and largely white underparts, with darker markings around the head and under the wings. Its bill is strong and hooked, and its long, broad wings give it a steady, languid flight. It is usually identified at sea by its relatively large size, dark-and-white plumage, straight-winged flight, and dark cap contrasting with the pale underside. It is rarely seen close enough for detailed field marks.
value.rangeHabitat: The Tahiti Petrel breeds on mountainous and forested islands, using soil burrows, rock crevices, and cavities beneath vegetation. Breeding sites may range from low rocky islets to high mountain slopes. At sea it occupies warm tropical and subtropical waters of the Pacific. In the Costa Rica region, it is an uncommon offshore visitor rather than a breeding or land-based species. Reliable records occur in the Pacific Ocean west and southwest of Costa Rica, including waters associated with Isla del Coco, and birds may also be encountered during pelagic surveys farther offshore.
value.migrationStatus: The species is a wide-ranging disperser rather than a strongly seasonal migrant. After breeding, individuals spread across the tropical Pacific and reach the eastern tropical Pacific, including offshore waters of Costa Rica. It is rarely observed from the mainland coast and has no known breeding population in Costa Rica.
value.breeding: Tahiti Petrels usually breed in isolated colonies on tropical Pacific islands. Pairs nest in burrows or rock cavities, often in forest, dense vegetation, mountain ridges, or steep rocky terrain. One white egg is laid, and both adults share incubation and chick-rearing duties. Incubation is about 54–56 days in studied colonies, while chicks may remain in the nest for roughly 110–120 days. Adults generally visit colonies at night, which makes the species difficult to survey.
value.dietFeeding: The diet consists mainly of squid and fish, with other marine prey such as crustaceans also taken. Studies indicate that the species often feeds on deep-water organisms and may seize dead or weakened prey floating at the surface. It forages over open tropical ocean, sometimes working around productive areas where prey is concentrated. Like other procellariiform seabirds, it can travel long distances from breeding islands while searching for food.
value.behavior: Tahiti Petrels are powerful ocean fliers that often travel with slow, gliding wingbeats and shallow banking movements. They are mainly pelagic and spend extended periods away from land. Breeding adults are strongly nocturnal at colonies, reducing exposure to predators, and may call near nest sites after dark. At sea they are usually solitary or seen in small numbers, although they can join mixed-species seabird groups where food is available.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered to be declining, although trends are poorly known in several breeding regions. Surveys in the eastern tropical Pacific indicated a substantial reduction between the late 1980s and late 1990s, and declines have been reported at some island colonies.
conservation.threats: Introduced predators, especially feral cats and rats, can kill adults, chicks, and eggs at breeding colonies. Dogs and pigs may also disturb or dig into nests. Artificial lights can disorient fledglings and adults near settlements, causing collisions and grounding. Habitat disturbance and mining affect some colonies in New Caledonia, while localized harvesting has been reported in parts of French Polynesia. Offshore threats may include incidental capture in fisheries, although the scale for this species is not well established.
conservation.howToHelp: Protecting breeding islands through removal or control of introduced cats, rats, dogs, and pigs is a major conservation priority. Safeguarding native forest and nesting habitat, reducing artificial lighting near colonies, and monitoring remote breeding sites can improve survival. In Costa Rica, observers can contribute by submitting well-documented pelagic records from the Pacific, especially around Isla del Coco, while avoiding disturbance to any storm-driven or grounded birds and supporting marine wildlife monitoring.
